entries.title: Man, 40, fatally shot leaving Grand Crossing gas station Saturday
entries.summary: <p>A 40-year-old man was fatally shot early Saturday by someone who approached him as he left a gas station in Grand Crossing, Chicago police said.</p><p>Police said the shooting took place along the 7100 block of South Vincennes Avenue at about 4:48 a.m.</p><p>The unidentified victim suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>Police said the alleged shooter fled in a dark SUV. Area 1 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Mark Scheifele's huge game exposes Blackhawks' lack of shutdown forward
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> have had no answers for Jets star Mark Scheifele for years, and they had none again Saturday.</p><p>A heroic effort by Scheifele rallied the Jets from a four-goal deficit to a 5-4 shootout victory, extending their voodoo-filled winning streak to six games and dealing the Hawks their 10th loss in their last 12.</p><p>Scheifele scored the Jets’ first goal, then took advantage of Hawks goalie Spencer Knight’s stick getting stuck in the boards — a very unlucky break — to set up Kyle Connor to cut the deficit to 4-2 by the second intermission.</p><p>Early in the third, Scheifele deftly tossed the puck into the crease to enable a power-play goal by Cole Perfetti. Late in the third, he showed great vision and sense of timing to hit Gabriel Vilardi in the crease for the tying goal. And in the shootout, he sniped the corner over Knight to convert his attempt.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Jets goal: Gabriel Vilardi with a late goal to tie it. <a href="https://t.co/SCW9xLMrZN">pic.twitter.com/SCW9xLMrZN</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2121742123963760725?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 14, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>It was an MVP-caliber, four-point performance. From a Hawks perspective, however, it wasn’t anything they hadn’t seen before.</p><p>Scheifele now has 46 points in 51 career games against the Hawks, including a whopping 14 in their last six meetings. Many of those have come in clutch fashion, too.</p><p>In October 2024, he scored with 64 seconds left in regulation and again 38 seconds into overtime to flip a 1-0 Hawks lead into a 2-1 Jets victory.</p><p>In March 2026, he assisted on a goal with 39 seconds left in regulation and scored two minutes into overtime to flip a 2-1 Hawks lead into a 3-2 Jets victory.</p><p>Despite seeing it over and over, the Hawks can’t seem to stop it. Anecdotes such as those reiterate just how desperately they lack a true shutdown forward capable of stifling opposing stars on a nightly basis.</p><p>Granted, they also lack a reliable six-man defensive corps — although Alex Vlasic and Ian Cole were excellent Saturday — and a second offensive star to complement Connor Bedard, among many other things. Their holes are plentiful.</p><p>Obviously, a Selke Trophy-caliber center would transform the Hawks’ lineup, but those types of players are rare. The Hawks are trying to develop their own in Anton Frondell, whom they believe might become their next Jonathan Toews. That’s why they’re stubbornly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/13/how-blackhawks-rookie-anton-frondell-keeps-friendship-alive-with-jets-rookie-viggo-bjorck" target="_blank" >keeping him at center</a> instead of moving him to Bedard’s wing.</p><p>But even somebody such as former Hawks forward Jason Dickinson would make a big difference. Although Dickinson’s game was one-dimensional and he contributed little offense, he could — and, with the Oilers, still can — shut down opponents at an elite level.</p><p>Dickinson was also a critical component of the Hawks’ penalty kill and six-on-five defense, which is notable, considering the events of Saturday.</p><p>He wasn’t great on faceoffs, but he was respectable. The Hawks, who won only 19 of 60 draws Saturday and rank last in the NHL in faceoff winning percentage by a wide margin, could use that, too.</p><p>I wrote two games into this season how the Hawks seemed to be missing the stability Dickinson, Ilya Mikheyev and Connor Murphy provided, and I’ve had that same thought countless times since then.</p><p>Those veterans kept the team afloat in the defensive zone perhaps more than anyone appreciated at the time. They also made it a no-brainer decision for Hawks coaches about which line and defensive pairing would handle the toughest matchups in every game.</p><p>Without their services this season, coach Jeff Blashill has shifted around those responsibilities on a game-to-game basis, and he hasn’t found a consistent formula.</p><p>It was strange that Frondell, who did a good job in a heavy matchup role against Scheifele on Oct. 15, barely saw Scheifele on Saturday. Instead, Bedard’s line received the most ice time against Scheifele, and an injury to Tyler Bertuzzi in the third period further tilted the Hawks’ disadvantage in that matchup.</p>

entries.title: Bulls see travel squeeze in wake of longest ground stoppage in 25 years
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS – The longest nationwide ground stoppage in 25 years impacted the flight plans of the entire country in the last 48 hours.</p><p>The Bulls were no exceptions to that.</p><p>Scheduled to leave Chicago after their Friday win against Atlanta and head to the Twin Cities for a back-to-back with Minnesota, the team found out afterwards that they would instead leave Saturday morning. Even that was delayed slightly, however, with the team getting in around noon.</p><p>Luckily, because it was a back-to-back it didn’t alter a ton of game preparation. In the normal second game of a back-to-back, teams often have no morning shootaround, instead watching film at the hotel and possibly going through a mock walkthrough in a hotel ballroom.</p><p>Bulls coach Tiago Splitter simply pushed the schedule to pre-game at the arena. The team had a film session 35 minutes before tip-off and went through strategy at that time.</p><p>It was still a first for Splitter, however.</p><p>“It’s kind of weird to travel the morning of a game,” he said. “At least for me it’s a first.”</p><p>What Splitter made sure of was his team didn’t use it as an excuse, especially because dozens of teams across the NBA, NFL and college football had to deal with the travel issues.</p><p>“Other than that it’s a back-to-back,” Splitter added. “You gotta bring the energy. Your legs are going to be a little heavier than normal but just take it like another game.”</p><p>As far as the rest of the three-city trip, it was business as usual. The Bulls were expected to fly to Cleveland Sunday afternoon and have the usual morning shootaround in preparation for the Monday night game with the Cavaliers.</p><p></p><p><b>Staying the course</b></p><p></p><p>It would have been easy for splinters to start coming to the surface in the locker room with the dismal 1-9 start, but as the win over the Hawks showed the locker room remains patient with the process.</p><p>“We’re doing a good job of that,” veteran Jalen Smith said when asked if the locker room showed any chemistry rough patches. “We’re a young team, we’re really connected with one another, you know. Pretty much everyone is around the same age, give or take a few guys, so we have a great relationship. We knew it was going to be hard – whole new front office, whole new coaching staff – we just got to put together wins. The NBA is a big boys’ league, you lose, you lose, but you want to go out fighting.</p><p>“I think we’re making the right strides. Everyone is trusting the process, everyone is putting in extra work, watching film, making sure we’re correcting our mistakes.”</p><p></p><p><b>The training room</b></p><p></p><p>Smith (left finger sprain) was injured late in the overtime win over Atlanta and wasn’t able to go on Saturday. The good news was it seemed like a minor setback rather than anything long term, according to the center.</p><p>As far as Nic Claxton and how the Bulls are going to handle playing him in back-to-backs after he missed the first three weeks of the season with a tweaked hamstring? They’re not. For the time being he will not play in the second game of a back-to-back.</p><p></p><p><b>Where’s Lenny?</b></p><p></p><p>Leonard Miller was one of the few positive surprises late last season and seemed to be capitalizing on that momentum throughout the summer and into the preseason, but after a subpar start to his season, he’s currently out of the rotation for the time being.</p><p>Shooting 18.5% and 43.4% from the field didn’t help.</p><p>“He had an outstanding summer for us, preseason,” Splitter said. “Now he’s a little bit out of the rotation. He didn’t start the season the way he wanted, but hopefully he can bounce back and play the way he was during the summer.”</p>

entries.title: Cancellations, delays at O'Hare, Midway continue Saturday in fallout from FAA ground stop

Federal officials said travel should be back to normal by Sunday.</p><p>For United passenger Abdul Sankoh of Manassas, Virginia, the disruption meant spending more than seven hours aboard a plane stuck on the tarmac, missing his scheduled arrival at Dulles International Airport in Washington, D.C., and spending another four hours Saturday morning waiting in line to speak with an airline customer service representative.</p><p>Sankoh had been scheduled to depart O'Hare Airport for Dulles at 2:21 p.m. Friday. entries.title: Cary-Grove forces four turnovers, rushes for 431 yards to beat St. Francis
entries.summary: <p>In Cary and Fox River Grove, kids grow up counting the days till they can suit up in Penn State-inspired navy-blue-and-white uniforms to play on a pristine grass football field with old-school goalposts.</p><p>Junior lineman Caleb Wright was one of those kids hoping to add to Cary-Grove’s tradition.</p><p>‘‘It’s like nothing else, if I’m being honest,’’ Wright said. ‘‘We all dreamed about this before we go to sleep, and it’s all seeming to come true now. We’ve just got to keep executing, getting better every single day.’’</p><p>The No. 25 Trojans have another week to get better after turning four takeaways into 27 points and knocking out defending champion St. Francis 55-36 in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class5a-illinois-2026" target="_blank" >Class 5A</a> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/11/13/2026-ihsa-state-football-quarterfinal-playoff-scores" target="_blank" >quarterfinal</a> Saturday in Cary.</p><p>Cary-Grove (10-2) will host Sycamore (9-4) next weekend in search of its fourth state-championship berth since 2018.</p><p>‘‘For many years, the semifinals were the standard here,’’ Trojans coach Brad Seaburg said. ‘‘And now that standard has really been elevated. And so the kids know that, yeah, the semifinals is where we want to be right now. But we want to keep going.’’</p><p>Thanks to a big first half by the defense, they will.</p><p>Junior Zach Witt had two interceptions, and sophomore Leo Zavala picked off a pass and recovered a fumble forced by Wright.</p><p>‘‘Our game plan was just play as a team and just not try to be a hero,’’ Witt said. ‘‘We had our D-line having great pressure, our linebackers filling holes, our corners really going after those wide receivers all night.’’</p><p>The turnovers and takeaways were unusual for both teams, Seaburg noted.</p><p>‘‘We have not [been creating turnovers], and they have not turned the ball over like that all year,’’ Seaburg said. ‘‘So we did some things to them that [caused them to do things] they haven’t been doing all year. . . . I think that’s a testament to our defense.’’</p><p>‘‘I give a lot of credit to those coaches and those kids,’’ St. Francis coach Bob McMillen said. ‘‘They literally beat the crap out of us. And you can’t turn the ball over four times against a team like that.’’</p><p>This was as inexperienced a team as Seaburg has had in his 16 seasons. The Trojans had to replace four starters on the offensive line and both tight ends — all key cogs in their triple-option attack.</p><p>But they did have one key player with experience back: junior quarterback Jackson Berndt.</p><p>‘‘He’s got two years of varsity experience,’’ Seaburg said. ‘‘And as a freshman, he took quite a few snaps in the playoffs. He’s a cool cat back there. Very composed.’’</p><p>Berndt ran 11 times for 124 yards and a touchdown. Senior Shamarion Prude had 13 carries for 170 yards and a touchdown, and sophomore Luke Ceresa ran nine times for 59 yards and three scores.</p><p>‘‘We just have a rotation going,’’ Ceresa said. ‘‘ ‘Sham’ and I, we switch every three [plays]. . . . I think we complement each other great, and the offensive line just had a great push on all the runs.’’</p><p>Berndt threw one pass, which fell incomplete, and Cary-Grove ran 42 times for 431 yards. The Trojans led 34-14 at halftime and 41-14 midway through the third quarter.</p><p>For St. Francis (7-6), junior quarterback Jadon Wilson was 16-for-28 for 230 yards and four touchdowns — two each to Blayke Lohmann and Noah Turner — with three interceptions and a lost fumble. He also ran 16 times for 92 yards.</p><p>Tivias Caldwell Jr. had 25 carries for 127 yards and a touchdown for the Spartans.</p>

entries.title: Notre Dame has no trouble with visiting Boston College
entries.summary: <p>SOUTH BEND, Ind. — CJ Carr passed for 217 yards and two touchdowns, and No. 3 Notre Dame showed no letdown after knocking off Miami last week, beating Boston College 41-7 on Saturday.</p><p>Notre Dame beat then-No. 1 Miami 31-24 last Saturday. The Fighting Irish (9-1), who are No. 5 in the College Football Playoff rankings, returned Saturday and rolled to a 31-0 halftime lead.</p><p>Fighting Irish coach Marcus Freeman said his team did a great job of blocking out noise all week about 1993, when Notre Dame beat No. 1 Florida State but then lost to Boston College at home the next week.</p><p>“I thought the leadership was spot on this week, and I thought the guys understood the challenge they had in front of us, and they went out and played that way,” Freeman said. “I think you can look at the product that you saw on the field today and say they prepared the right way, they had the right mindset, but I think every day it’s a choice. It’s a choice you make.”</p><p>Carr completed 20-of-28 passes, including a 26-yard TD pass to Micah Gilbert and a 13-yard scoring strike to Jordan Faison. He praised the team's focus against Boston College after the Miami victory.</p><p>“We try and do this with losses a lot, but what can we take from that game against Miami into this next week. You want to flush the feelings and the urge to stay in ... that moment," Carr said. "I think we can take the detail and the preparation that we had from that week and use that to propel us into this week and weeks beyond.”</p><p>Freshman running back Jonaz Walton gained 141 yards on 15 carries and scored on a 1-yard run. Nolan James Jr. added 73 yards rushing and a 10-yard TD. They replaced NFL first-round picks Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price.</p><p>“They’re just continuously getting better,” Freeman said. “They’re continuously working together. They’re seeing things that maybe they didn’t see a month ago or two months ago.”</p><p>Jaylen Sneed scored a 1-yard scoop-and-score touchdown off a fumble forced by Boubacar Traore. The Fighting Irish limited Boston College to 136 yards of total offense.</p><p>Boston College (4-6) cashed in on Carr’s second interception of the season. K.P. Price picked off the pass at the Notre Dame 27. Three plays later, the Eagles’ Bo MacCormack III powered into the end zone from the 3 for the touchdown.</p><p><b>The Takeaway</b></p><p>Defense opened the door for a 24-0 domination by Notre Dame in the second quarter. Boston College had minus-10 yards of total offense in the second quarter.</p><p>Boston College added to its Atlantic Coast Conference-best mark for interceptions when Price intercepted Carr's pass. The Eagles lead the ACC with 13 interceptions. Price has four.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Boston College: Hosts Syracuse next Saturday.</p><p>Notre Dame: Hosts SMU next Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Man, 21, dies after paraglider crashes in Plainfield
entries.summary: <p>A 21-year-old man died Saturday after his paraglider crashed into a farm field in Plainfield following an apparent in-flight emergency, police said.</p><p>Police received a call at 2:57 p.m. about the crash that occurred near 127th Street and Ridge Road, according to a news release.</p><p>Witnesses at the scene assisted the pilot until Oswego paramedics arrived and attempted lifesaving measures, police said.</p><p>Giovanni Lopez, of Woodridge, was pronounced dead at the scene by the Kendall County coroner's office, police said.</p><p>Plainfield police detectives and the Kendall County coroner's office are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Life without Caleb Wilson carries on for Bulls, evident by a second win
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS – There’s a next-man-up mentality that most professional franchises need to have.</p><p>At least the ones that have any hopes of surviving a significant injury to the roster.</p><p>The Bulls displayed that in the wake of prized rookie Caleb Wilson being lost for up to six weeks because of undergoing right hand surgery, beating Atlanta in overtime on Friday and showing up a night later with by far their best basketball of the season in upsetting the Timberwolves 117-106.</p><p>Not a bad response at all.</p><p>“Our jobs are on the line too,” reserve guard Buddy Hield said very matter-of-factly after the latest win. “The organization is in the position where they’re trying to figure out where they are moving in the next direction. No disrespect to Caleb, but we have guys that have been in the league for more than four or five years and we understand what it takes to win. Putting all the BS aside and being a good teammate, going out to compete, making winning plays and that translates into wins.”</p><p>Words that followed up actions from Hield, as it was the likes of him, Patrick Williams and Tre Jones that came off the bench, withstood a third-quarter rally by the home team, and helped the Bulls to a 3-9 record.</p><p>Hield and Jones each had 16 points, while Williams added 15 points and was a plus-10 in plus/minus.</p><p>“We’re winners,” Williams said of the bench mentality. “That’s what winners do. Do whatever you need to when your name is called. Whatever it looks like, whether it’s scoring, rebounding, whatever it is.”</p><p>That was the latest known for the Bulls.</p><p>The unknown is how will the 20-year-old Wilson handle being a spectator and not a key foundation piece until possibly Christmas time?</p><p>If it’s up to the Bulls, it won’t be him overthinking the setback on his own.</p><p>Coach Tiago Splitter went into a bit more detail on Saturday about the plan surrounding Wilson and how the organization wants to handle his rehabilitation. It involves being around the team as much as possible, likely starting after this three-city road trip.</p><p>“He’s not traveling right now because he still has stitches and he can’t sweat yet, so a couple days off, but once we come back (from this road trip) he’s going to be around the team and travel with the team,” the coach said.</p><p>Which Splitter, the medical staff and the front office all deem key in his comeback.</p><p>“I think it’s extremely important just to be a part of the film sessions, the meetings, be on the bench, be part of the goods and bads of the team throughout those games,” Splitter said. “It’s also going to give him a different perspective on not having the pressure of the game and the open mind to just watch everything, try to learn and absorb everything from those situations.”</p><p>Considering the Bulls were near the bottom of the league in offensive efficiency and at the bottom in defense, it’s not like life without Wilson would do damage to either of those statistical categories.</p><p>The two major gut-punches specifically center around Wilson.</p><p>First and foremost, it’s a month to six weeks of development that every rookie needs, especially one that was being counted on as heavily as Wilson was. The other slap is Wilson’s Rookie of the Year candidacy and how important it was to him.</p><p>Since first being drafted back in June, Wilson has not been shy in admitting that he not only wanted to win the Rookie of the Year trophy of a very talented 2026 draft but wanted to personally outperform any rookie in the class whenever he faced them.</p><p>This setback puts him near the back of the line behind the likes of Cameron Boozer, Darius Acuff Jr., Yaxel Lendeborg, Darryn Peterson and AJ Dybantsa.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Wedding invitation leads to unpleasant breakup
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I dated a man for 16 months. We spent a lot of time together. We traveled, enjoyed many sports events and shared some mutual friends who actually introduced us.</p><p>One evening, we were out for dinner with another couple of his friends. During the conversation, the woman asked him if I was going to his daughter's wedding. His response shocked me. He shook his head, saying, "I don't think so." I remained calm, but I felt hurt. It wasn't because I "had" to go to the wedding but because he didn't even discuss it with me.</p><p>I was embarrassed, so I excused myself from the table. When I returned, I asked for my jacket. His response was, "This isn't going to end well." I asked him if that was a threat, to which he did not respond. I called a ride share and left.</p><p>The next day, he delivered all my belongings from his apartment. Over — just like that! No explanation. He did scream at me while dropping off my things, about why I thought I should be invited when I had never met his daughter. I couldn't speak at the time because I was dumbfounded. A few days later, we had a text exchange. I asked him about a golfing buddy of his being invited. He said yes. I said, "He never met your daughter." Phone silence.</p><p>He later invited me to go to lunch but said, "No crying." I declined and said, "I don't want to eat, and I don't want to be friends with someone who treats me so horribly." A week or two later, I got an email saying, "This is my last communication ever." I don't think he had to announce it, but OK. It's been a year now, but it still bothers me. Am I wrong? — <i>MAKING NO SENSE IN MINNESOTA</i></p><p><b>DEAR MAKING NO SENSE:</b> The man you were dating had his reasons for not inviting the woman he had been seeing for 16 months. If I had been sitting in your position, rather than pouting and retreating, I would have asked him why he hadn't mentioned such an important milestone and let him explain it in front of his friends. That said, the romance is over. Let it go. To say that he was controlling and insensitive would be an understatement. In my opinion, you dodged a nasty bullet.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I belong to a group of 10 women who meet once a month. We're all seniors, and most, but not all, of the women have husbands. I'd like to set up a dinner for couples so we can meet each other's husbands. Should I invite only those with spouses? Invite everyone, but ask that the singles bring a date? Just let the singles come solo? — <i>HESITANT HOSTESS</i></p><p><b>DEAR HOSTESS:</b> Why would you need to exclude the single women as you meet one another's husbands? I suspect they, too, are curious about their friends' spouses. Make sure the singles know they are welcome to bring a date if they want to, but they, not you, should decide whether mingling with a roomful of couples will make them uncomfortable.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

Todd Christofferson.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Another letter submitted to Sargus came from Dennis Johnson, who wrote that he’s known Wade Christofferson “in several capacities, including as his bishop . . . as a close friend, and as a fellow volunteer in community and church service activities.”</p><p>“There is no minimizing the seriousness of the offense for which Wade now stands before the Court,” Johnson wrote, adding that over months of jail visits, he’s “observed genuine remorse for his actions.”</p><p>Another letter writer is a brother-in-law to Wade Christofferson who noted in his correspondence that he’s a professor emeritus at Brigham Young University, a Mormon institution.</p><p>An attorney for Wade Christofferson notes in recently filed court records: “The letters do not contradict the guilty plea or negate the harm done to the victims. entries.title: Lt. Gov.-elect Christian Mitchell blazes new Illinois trail: 'I realize whose shoulders I stand on'
entries.summary: <p>Democrats’ blue tsunami on election night ushered in a wave of “firsts” across the nation, from the first Black woman elected governor, Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms, to the first Muslim person elected to the U.S. Senate, Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed.</p><p>It also washed over Illinois, which will become the first state <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/juliana-strattons-win-marks-historic-first-for-women-of-color-in-national-politics" target="_blank" ><u>to send two women of color to the U.S. Senate</u></a> when outgoing Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton is sworn in alongside incumbent Sen. Tammy Duckworth in January.</p><p>Stratton’s ascent allowed for another new trail to be blazed in her office, which will be filled by Christian Mitchell, the first Black man elected as Illinois’ lieutenant governor.</p><p>“I feel incredibly honored by it,” Mitchell told the Sun-Times. “I realize whose shoulders I stand on. I realize we lost Jesse Jackson this year, who talked about keeping hope alive and did so much work for the vote, and John Lewis, and so many people.”</p><p>But first on the 40-year-old former legislator’s mind, while addressing a packed Navy Pier ballroom after declaring <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/governor-illinois-jb-pritzker-darren-bailey-collin-corbett-results" target="_blank" ><u>victory alongside Gov. JB Pritzker</u></a>, were his mother, Deb Gist; his late grandmother, Lilly Mae Gist; and his late grandfather and “hero,” James Gist, who served as a U.S. Army sergeant.</p><p>“At the time he went out to fight for this country in Korea, we did not have the Civil Rights Act, and he did not have his rights of the franchise guaranteed. So on a personal level, I feel that weight,” Mitchell said the day after making history.</p><p>“Juliana blazed a trail here as the first Black woman to be lieutenant governor. The fact that we have so many of these firsts in 2026 shows that we still have a ways to go, so I’m very grateful,” he said. “But we have so much more work to do, and ultimately, regardless of your color, your creed, where you live, I want to be a lieutenant governor for everyone in the way that JB has been a governor for everybody.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Breaking new ground in an office with no defined responsibilities beyond being a heartbeat away from becoming governor, Mitchell’s position as lieutenant governor-elect takes on enhanced significance as Pritzker considers running for president.</p><p>Mitchell’s job description will shift considerably if the third-term governor hits the 2028 campaign trail — and he’ll make even more history if Pritzker actually wins the White House.</p><p>Mitchell says that hasn’t affected the way he approaches the office, and the prospect of becoming the state’s first Black governor is not what drew him back to public service after a two-year stint as vice president of civic engagement at the University of Chicago.</p><p>“I've always said and always been taught by my mentors, including JB, that if you do the job that you have in front of you, the future takes care of itself,” Mitchell said, hardly downplaying Pritzker’s potential national ambition.</p><p>“It's good that people look at that and say, ‘Hey, with everything broken in Washington, we want that kind of leadership to go national.’ That's great,” Mitchell said. “It's also why it's great that he won a third term. So for me, as his governing partner and somebody who every day approaches his job with a high level of seriousness and a focus on the kind of people who raised me — single moms, union workers, farmers — I'm going to do that, no matter what's potentially happening.</p><p>“And ultimately it's why I'm so glad to be running with somebody who said, ‘Hey, I want to do this again, I want to run for a third term.’ I want to keep the work going,” said Mitchell, who has been one of Pritzker’s closest confidants since the governor was first elected in 2018.</p><p>The Bronzeville resident became the youngest state representative at the time he was elected from the 26th District in 2012 at age 26, serving three terms before being named a deputy governor in Pritzker’s administration in 2019.</p><p>Mitchell shepherded Pritzker’s signature $45 billion capital infrastructure program through the General Assembly and ran point on other key legislation, including landmark climate legislation aiming to wean Illinois off fossil fuels.</p><p>Mitchell, a former adviser to Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle, also helped manage the rollout of the state’s recreational cannabis industry, while leading <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/opinion/2020/7/3/21312061/coronavirus-illinois-medical-supplies-wild-west-competition-face-masks-christian-mitchell-stockpiles" target="_blank" ><u>frenzied procurement efforts</u></a> for badly needed supplies in the darkest early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>An Illinois Air National Guard first lieutenant by part-time trade and an amateur boxer by hobby, Mitchell says he’s excited to get back to the Capitol.</p><p>“Getting out on the trail was really the most invigorating for me,” he said. “The challenges are common, but so are the hopes, so is the decency. I'm a Black man from the South Side of Chicago, and I'm going to places where often people don't look like me, and I still felt incredibly welcome.</p><p>“In the state, if you get it right and you can convince colleagues to do it, you can move pretty quickly... You can do things pretty quickly if you pull the right people together.”</p>
